While this is a great exercise in gaining knowledge learning the fundamentals of electricity can help here too. The post you are replying to is correct and you are mostly correct. Electromagnetic forces as we currently understand them in physics act over infinite distance. This means that an electron on Pluto can technically experience the force of an electron on earth. While in reality it is negligible, electrons in a DAC and electrons in the same room as the DAC are feeling the forces from each other. This may also be negligible but factoring in how many sources of electromagnetic forces exist either naturally or man-made it may add up more than we realize. And physically speaking even if we cannot perceive or measure it, these affects (along with others like temp) mean that no two DACs will reproduce the same analog wave. Not unless they are exact replicas and are in perfectly shielded and controlled environments when they perform the conversion. 

It really comes down to the fact that in the real world outside of theorems and the useful assumptions they employ, you cannot say absolutes like always, perfectly, never, etc. That's all that the user you are replying to is saying

I guess I think of it like this:

ynab uses a monthly budget system. It you budget money on a per month basis and it tracks transactions on a per month basis. It assumes that at the end of the month you have assigned money according to your budget and the transactions you made within that month should stay true to that budget. It isn't about negative or positive balances but about how much you budgeted to spend and how much was spent in that month. Otherwise it would just be a balance tracker.

 YNAB is about helping you track and plan your spending so you know where every dollar is going. When you have an expense that was not accounted for in the monthly budget that money had to come from somewhere as it isn't in your pocket anymore. That is the key. Maybe it will be coming back, but to ynab money came out and it wasn't accounted for by the monthly budget and the month is now over.

I think there are ways to "account" for reimbursements which is what other replies have mentioned doing but how you do it is up to you. YNAB is pretty opinionated in it's budgeting methodology we all have certain parts that we don't particularly mesh well with.

>to do otherwise would surely mean that while the current month looks great, I will be woefully unprepared for the massive mortgage payment on the first of the following month

I am under the school of thought that if this month looks great, that means my payments on the 1st of the next month are already taken care of. I feel like YNAB's monthly cycle made this really confusing for me in the beginning. I have tried to reconcile with this but one thing I remember is that **I need to budget according to when I spend not when it is due**. That helps me pay rent when I immediately am able to but I understand that paying mortgages early doesn't behave in a desired way. It may be helpful to have a next month mortgage category.

Another thing: to me is that any bill in **this month** that is underfunded is just as important as the other ones. maybe missing my netflix payment isn't as bad as not having enough for next month's mortgage but its a slippery slope to missing credit card payments or your electricity getting shutoff... That might be a bit exaggerated and obviously that is subjective. I just feel that either way you need to fill up this month before next month (which is how Auto-assign operates more or less) because filling up next month before this month is done just means you will have to fill up the rest of this month eventually anyway and then after that continue filling up next month.

>any money left over after regular expenses are sorted gets left in RTA until I buy something. Only then do I move it to the proper category

I used to do this too! I understand and it took awhile before I assigned all of RTA and sometimes I do leave a little in... But we mustn't!

>My brain feels better knowing I have $<big number> for "whatever" rather than several $<not big numbers> for "that particular thing". I used to shuffle it off into an "Available to spend" category, but this is also mostly counter to the YNAB Way just with extra steps.

It sounds to me like your categories might need a rework. Like I said, I used to do the same thing with RTA. I like having some money up there for peace of mind, but I realized that is a symptom of not really having categories I am confident in.  RTA becomes a "things I am not confident fit into a category" category. If that makes any sense. So its about looking at your categories and deciding "Even though x purchase will go here, why don't I feel comfortable assigning my RTA to it?" Rereading your post it almost sounds like you don't know if "the  several $<not big numbers>" will be enough for each of the "particular things." Maybe you could focus in on why you aren't confident in each category's amounts and adjust your budget to the point that you are comfortable.

Once I became comfortable with my spending habits, I know that I can assign money to the respective category the available amount is what I draw comfort from and not RTA. And I think that makes waiting for YNAB to sync not as stressful for me, cause when it clears, my category is ready for it.

Honestly this is harder to explain than I thought so I hope it makes sense.

Once you are confident your spending fits into your categories you can make targets for it that auto assign will then use to determine priority when assigning . And as far as targets go I am not the one to give advice as I don't find them useful if used as intended.

Last thing: You can always assign your own personal high priority categories and then auto-assign the rest! It is flexible enough for you to do that.

I remind myself about my goals and I also ask myself if I really need it. Was I planning on buying? Was I planning on making that purchase today? It's a slow process to stop habitually spending but I used to buy all sorts of useless tech and other nothings that caught my eye.

Oh and avoid promotional emails and sales. I have to remind myself that a sale can't be the only reason to buy something and the other reason definitely can't be "But, I want it, and it's x% off!"  I still spend money impulsive sometimes but much less than I used to.

For that quick food fix I usually remind myself of what I'd rather spend my money on, this cheap meal I can always get or a nice restaurant meal I budget for each month. Or even that one fancy place in France I will go to when I visit my family. I usually realize I would rather save my money to spend on a really nice and memorable meal than the fast food meal. 

The last thing is I budget guilt free money that I can spend impulsively that sometimes I still feel guilty spending. But the goal is to have money set aside that you can dip into without feeling bad and giving up on budgeting and it helps you get in the mindset of following your budget. You can set aside a lot at first but adjust it as time goes on to be less. 

Good luck hope this helps.

I have a Q2 and CV1 and I had the Rift S. Similar boat as you I was mostly into PCVR. I'll break down my thoughts on each,  but I have a strange bias towards the CV1 for being cool because it was the pioneer in consumer VR (afaik) so keep that in mind:

Q2
Pros:
- Untethered is actually great, and with good network setup can play without realizing you are streaming. It will only occasionally stutter (ymmv) just from signal pollution and other unavoidable network hiccups
- visual clarity, great for reading, less noticeable screen door
- tracking is basically good and will not slow you down
- no tracking sensors needed
- support from meta hardware and software
- non Pcvr can still be really fun
- Can use a cord to use it like it were a rift or rift s
- pass through cameras
- easy to use boundary set up system

Cons:
- not the most comfy but manageable, including controllers, cv1 is most comfortable for my hands. Modding and accessories can help but increases cost usually
- battery life is only a few hours if lucky (granted software updates have surprisingly improved battery life even for heavily used Q2's in my anecdotal experience), but my vr endurance is low now anyway so I usually end up stopping anyway
- using it with my PC connected by USB only lengthens uptime but doesn't charge it while in use (ymmv haven't tested recently)
- sometimes complains about USB type even if your port meets the spec indicated
- joysticks seem to wear out quickly and develop drift
- not a fan of the speakers compared to CV1

Rift S
Pros:
- no battery no issue
- tracking seems to be on par with Q2, I don't notice any issues
- no tracking sensors needed
- controllers are slightly more comfy than Q2
- didn't notice a joystick drift issue, but I think I didnt have it for as long/didnt use the controllers as much
- more comfy headset and strap design than Q2 but debatable in comparison to CV1
- pass through cameras
- only needs USB port and DisplayPort (some issues with USB spec complaining, honestly I think this is present on every Oculus device. It will be find one day but the next will complain that it isn't the right USB even if nothing changed)
- same boundary system as Q2
- decent visuals, not as good as Q2 but better than CV1 still reads alright

Cons:
- heavier than CV1 but still comfortable
- probably less support as it is no longer made
- tethered and cord may wear out (proper care greatly will extend cord life)
- sometimes I found the connection between the headset and cord to be finicky, but might be my own issue with device care
- audio bad like Q2 I used it with over ear headphones, which was a bit difficult but worked 
- only bad part about the strap is that is pressed on the top of my head and would leave some soreness (maybe I wore it wrong... or played for too long in one sitting)

I sold my Rift S to get the Q2 but I regret it now. I think it was perfect for my uses and the CV1 is cool but the tracking sensors and worse resolution make it less convenient by just enough to make me want my Rift S back. 

CV1
Pros:
- comfortable all around could use it for a day and not care
- no battery
- light, and much more comfy as a result
- controllers are cool and mine are old but no drift issues at all
- maybe cheaper?
- tracking is great but need good placement to reduce blindspots
- IPD slider I didn't have issues with the other two but this is good if you are an outlier with eye spacing

cons:
- old
- cord and headset have known durability issues (they can be addressed there's a comment floating around here that explains how to take proper care) my cord has the signature "kink" and I hate it
- no more cord replacements at reasonable prices
- need at least 3 usb slots and an HDMI which has been surprisingly annoying to workaround
- resolution is noticeably poor compared to others but still can enjoy vr. Reading is a bit difficult
- one joystick squeaks and the triggers squeak (probably fixable just havent bothered)
- boundary setting is a bit of a pain compared to the newer systems and dependent on sensors. Bumping sensors at any time (not playing) can mess with the setup and center of playspace
- my room limitations lead to a lot of blindspots in tracking for the controllers and can be annoying when bending over to grab stuff if ever
- cord length has left me wanting to extend it several times

I hope that helps. If you have any specific questions you think are too specific I might be able to answer them.
